topHypothesis:
Hypothesis: Antibiotic treatment predisposes to C. difficile infection because it depletes specific bile acid-metabolizing taxa (e.g., Clostridium cluster XIVa/XIVb, Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae), converting the luminal bile acid pool from a predominantly secondary-bile-acid (inhibitory to C. difficile germination/outgrowth) composition to a primary-bile-acid-dominant composition that promotes C. difficile spore germination and vegetative growth.
Mechanism: Bile acid metabolism remodeling: antibiotic depletion of taxa capable of 7α-dehydroxylation reduces secondary bile acids (deoxycholate, lithocholate) that inhibit C. difficile germination and growth, while accumulation of primary bile acids (taurocholate, cholate) that trigger spore germination and support outgrowth; concurrently, reduced concentrations of the inhibitory secondary bile acids remove the chemical barrier to C. difficile expansion.
Predictions: Fecal secondary bile acid concentrations (deoxycholate, lithocholate) will be inversely correlated with C. difficile colonization in antibiotic-treated patients, and restoring secondary bile acids (e.g., via oral deoxycholate) will reduce or prevent colonization in a mouse model. | Antibiotic regimens that spare putative 7α-dehydroxylating taxa (or that do not reduce secondary bile acids) will confer lower CDI risk than regimens that deplete those taxa equivalently. | In vitro, C. difficile spore germination rates will be significantly higher in cecal/colonic extracts from antibiotic-treated animals than from untreated animals, and this effect will be reversed by exogenous secondary bile acid supplementation.
Expected relation: (i) Antibiotic treatment lowers fecal/cecal secondary bile acids (deoxycholate, lithocholate) and lowers the secondary:primary ratio relative to untreated controls; (ii) the secondary bile acid concentration (especially deoxycholate/lithocholate) is inversely correlated with C. difficile CFU burden across animals (Spearman r < -0.5, p<0.05); (iii) in vitro germination rate in cecal extracts from antibiotic-treated animals exceeds that in untreated extracts (>2-fold higher at 60-120 min); (iv) exogenous deoxycholate/lithocholate supplementation to extracts or to treated mice reverses the germination increase and reduces/prevents colonization (CFU reduction of ≥1.5 log10 relative to vehicle). (observable: Fecal/cecal concentrations of primary versus secondary bile acids (specifically cholate/taurocholate as primary, deoxycholate/lithocholate as secondary) and their temporal relationship to C. difficile spore germination/vegetative colonization in antibiotic-treated versus untreated hosts; plus the efficacy of exogenous secondary bile acid restoration in preventing colonization.).

Mechanism: Conjugation via self-transmissible and mobilizable plasmids (Type IV secretion systems, mating-pair formation) transfers ARGs between donor and recipient cells. (observable: The proportion of total ARG dissemination events in hospital-associated biofilms/surfaces that are attributable to conjugation (mating-dependent plasmid transfer) versus transformation or transduction, and whether conjugation frequency correlates with observed ARG spread in hospital microcosms with and without mating-pair-inhibitor intervention.).

topHypothesis:
Hypothesis: CRISPR-Cas9 off-target editing arises from the thermodynamic stability of the DNA-RNA (R-loop) heteroduplex, where mismatches in the PAM-distal region are tolerated better than in the PAM-proximal seed region because the binding energy landscape of R-loop nucleation and directional propagation determines whether the HNH nuclease domain is activated for cleavage.
Mechanism: The R-loop is nucleated at the PAM-proximal seed region and propagates directionally toward the PAM-distal end. Mismatches in the seed region disrupt nucleation and prevent R-loop formation, whereas mismatches in the distal region occur after the R-loop has already stabilized, so they are tolerated. The stability of the fully formed R-loop (correlating with cleavage efficiency at r=0.775-0.886) determines whether Cas9 reaches the conformational state required for HNH domain activation and double-strand cleavage. Off-targets occur when a partially or fully mismatched but sufficiently stable R-loop still triggers cleavage.
Predictions: Predicted off-target propensity should scale monotonically with computed R-loop thermodynamic stability across the guide | Introducing destabilizing mismatches in the PAM-distal region will reduce off-target editing less than equivalent mismatches in the PAM-proximal seed | Engineered guides that lower R-loop thermostability (melt-guides) will reduce cleavage of single-base mismatched sequences | Enhancing R-loop stability should proportionally increase off-target activity for any sequence context
Expected relation: (1) Off-target cleavage decreases monotonically as mismatch position moves from PAM-distal to PAM-proximal, i.e., a gradient where PAM-distal-mismatch off-targets (positions 1-9) yield higher retained cleavage than PAM-proximal-seed-mismatch off-targets (positions ~10-20). (2) Normalized cleavage efficiency correlates positively with computed R-loop ΔG stability with correlation coefficient in the range r≈0.775-0.886 for canonical guides. (3) Melt-guides with reduced thermostability show proportionally greater reduction of single-base-mismatch off-target cleavage than canonical guides. (observable: The differential off-target cleavage rate (measured as indel frequency or cleavage probability) as a function of the position of a single mismatched base pair along the guide-target alignment, and the correlation between computed R-loop thermodynamic stability and observed cleavage efficiency across engineered guides with modulated thermostability.).

agent: MSS/pMMR colorectal cancers lack responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade primarily because their low somatic mutation burden generates an insufficient neoantigen pool to prime and expand tumour-reactive T cells within the tumour microenvironment.

In MSS tumours, sparse neoantigens fail to generate a sufficiently strong T-cell response, so even if PD-1/PD-L1 is blocked, there are too few activated effector T cells to mediate tumour regression.

Among MSS/pMMR CRC patients, those with relatively higher (though still sub-MSI-H) mutation load or higher predicted neoantigen burden will show modestly better response rates to PD-1 blockade than those with very low mutation burden.
Combining checkpoint blockade with agents that increase neoantigen release (e.g., certain chemotherapies or radiation) will partially rescue responsiveness in MSS CRC.
Within MSS/pMMR CRC there should be a positive monotonic (dose-response) association between TMB/neoantigen load and CD8+ T-cell infiltration/expansion.
Within MSS/pMMR CRC there should be a positive monotonic (dose-response) association between TMB/neoantigen load and response to PD-1 blockade.
The predicted slope of the TMB-response association is modest because even the highest MSS TMB remains well below MSI-H levels.
MSI-H tumors with LOW TMB among the non-responders (i.e., the ~56% who do not respond in KEYNOTE-177) should show poor T-cell priming, linking TMB to response across the full CRC spectrum.

Hypothesis: MSS/pMMR colorectal cancers lack responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade primarily because their low somatic mutation burden generates an insufficient neoantigen pool to prime and expand tumour-reactive T cells within the tumour microenvironment.
Mechanism: Neoantigen-driven T-cell priming: In MSI-H/dMMR tumours, 10-100x higher mutation burden produces abundant neoantigens that are presented by MHC molecules, driving clonal expansion and infiltration of tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells. In MSS tumours, sparse neoantigens fail to generate a sufficiently strong T-cell response, so even if PD-1/PD-L1 is blocked, there are too few activated effector T cells to mediate tumour regression.

Expected relation: If the neoantigen-driven priming mechanism is correct, then within MSS/pMMR CRC there should be a positive monotonic (dose-response) association between TMB/neoantigen load and (i) CD8+ T-cell infiltration/expansion, and (ii) response to PD-1 blockade. However, the predicted slope is modest because even the highest MSS TMB remains well below MSI-H levels; the mechanism further predicts that MSI-H tumors with LOW TMB among the non-responders (i.e., the ~56% who do not respond in KEYNOTE-177) should show poor T-cell priming, linking TMB to response across the full CRC spectrum. topHypothesis:
Hypothesis: Acquired EGFR TKI resistance in NSCLC is primarily driven by secondary T790M gatekeeper mutations that restore EGFR signaling despite drug binding, with on-target resistance being the most prevalent single mechanism across cohorts.
Mechanism: A secondary point mutation (T790M) in the EGFR kinase domain alters the ATP-binding pocket conformation, reducing TKI binding affinity while preserving catalytic activity, thereby restoring downstream proliferative signaling even in the presence of the inhibitor.
Predictions: In larger multi-ethnic cohorts, T790M will remain the single most frequent acquired resistance mutation, present in a substantial plurality (approximately 40-55%) of TKI-resistant tumors. | T790M-positive resistant tumors will retain sustained phosphorylated EGFR and downstream ERK/AKT signaling in the presence of first-generation TKIs, whereas T790M-negative resistant tumors will show decoupled EGFR signaling. | Third-generation inhibitors (e.g., osimertinib) that covalently target T790M will show markedly higher and more durable responses specifically in patients whose resistance is T790M-positive versus T790M-negative.
Expected relation: If the hypothesis holds: (1) T790M frequency in the multi-ethnic cohort lands in the 40-55% band and is strictly greater than any single alternative mechanism (plurality); (2) T790M-positive resistant tumors show higher sustained pEGFR/pERK/pAKT under first-gen TKI than T790M-negative tumors; (3) osimertinib ORR in T790M-positive group exceeds T790M-negative group and in T790M-positive group exceeds historical non-TKI salvage rates. (observable: In a large multi-ethnic cohort of NSCLC patients with acquired resistance to first-generation EGFR TKIs, the proportion of resistant tumors harboring the secondary EGFR T790M gatekeeper mutation (measured by sensitive detection on re-biopsy at progression), and whether this proportion constitutes a strict plurality (single most frequent mechanism) over all other identified on-target and off-target resistance mechanisms combined, as well as whether T790M-positive resistant tumors retain sustained phosphorylated EGFR and downstream ERK/AKT signaling under TKI exposure and respond durably to osimertinib versus T790M-negative tumors.).
